Acantherpestes.note: A spiny millipede of the coal forests, up to thirty centimetres long -- smaller kin of the giant Arthropleura.

Acutiramus.note: A two-metre pterygotid sea scorpion with long pincers, among the largest arthropods of the Silurian.

Aegirocassis.note: A two-metre radiodont that filtered plankton with comb-like head limbs -- the gentle giant of the Early Ordovician Fezouata sea.

Alethopteris.note: Leaflets joined at their bases in long, strap-like rows -- the foliage of Medullosa, a seed fern whose seeds could be as large as a hen's egg.

Amphibamus.note: A ten-centimetre, salamander-shaped dissorophoid of the Pennsylvanian coal swamps, close to the ancestry of frogs and salamanders.

Amplectobelua.note: A radiodont with pincer-like grasping claws, one of the top predators of the Chengjiang sea.

Arandaspis.note: One of the oldest fishes with a bony skeleton: a jawless, finless, armoured swimmer of the Early Ordovician sea over central Australia.

Archaeolithophyllum.note: A leafy calcareous red alga that grew in thickets on Pennsylvanian shelves, building the 'phylloid algal mounds' that now hold oil.

Archaeothyris.note: One of the oldest synapsids, the line leading to mammals: a fifty-centimetre, lizard-shaped insect-eater found inside a fossil tree stump in Nova Scotia.

Armenoceras.note: An actinocerid nautiloid whose chambers are threaded by a thick, beaded siphuncle -- common in the warm Middle Ordovician seas of North China and Laurentia.

Autunia.note: A peltasperm seed fern whose leaf, long called Callipteris, is the classic sign of the base of the Permian in the red beds of Europe -- a plant of drier ground than the coal swamps.

Aysheaia.note: A velvet-worm-like lobopodian of the Burgess Shale, often found among the sponges it may have fed on.

Bailiella.note: An eyeless conocoryphid trilobite, of Middle Cambrian seas from North China to Avalonia and Bohemia.

Balanerpeton.note: A small land-going temnospondyl with an eardrum -- among the first tetrapods that could hear sound travelling through air.

Baltisphaeridium.note: A spiny acritarch -- the resting cyst of an Ordovician plankter -- used to date the Ordovician rocks of Baltica.

Blackwelderia.note: A damesellid trilobite with long spines fanning from its tail, typical of the Guzhangian seas of North China.

Buenellus.note: An olenellid trilobite, the commonest in the Sirius Passet beds on the northern edge of Cambrian Laurentia.

Cacops.note: A stocky, armour-backed amphibian with a large eardrum notch -- a land-going temnospondyl of the Early Permian, probably active at night.

Canadaspis.note: One of the commonest Burgess Shale arthropods: a bivalved, shrimp-like bottom-feeder that also lived in the Chengjiang sea.

Cardiola.note: A small, ribbed bivalve of the Silurian, abundant in the dark limestones of Bohemia and North Africa.

Ceraurus.note: A spiny cheirurid trilobite of the Trenton limestone seas, sometimes preserved with its legs.

Clymenia.note: A clymeniid ammonoid, whose siphuncle ran along the inner side of the shell -- the reverse of every other ammonoid -- living only in the last ten million years of the Devonian.

pbdb.homonym: Clymenia Savigny, a living maldanid polychaete; the ammonoid is Clymenia Muenster 1834

Coelurosauravus.note: The first gliding reptile: a lizard-sized weigeltisaurid that spread wings of skin on rods of bone growing from its flanks.

Crassigyrinus.note: A two-metre, big-mouthed stem tetrapod with tiny forelimbs -- back in the water, an ambush hunter of the Mississippian lakes.

Crotalocrinites.note: A Silurian crinoid whose arms fused into a web, a filtering fan; it grew in meadows on Silurian reefs.

Crussolum.note: One of the oldest centipedes, known from its legs in the Rhynie chert and the Gilboa forest -- already a venomous hunter of the early undergrowth.

Cyclolobus.note: One of the last of the Palaeozoic ammonoids, a Late Permian form with a finely frilled suture, from the Salt Range and Madagascar.

Damesella.note: A spiny-tailed damesellid trilobite of the late Middle Cambrian of North China and Korea.

Deiphon.note: A cheirurid trilobite with a swollen, globe-shaped head and long spines -- perhaps a swimmer in open water.

Delitzschala.note: One of the oldest winged insects, a palaeodictyopteran from the Early Carboniferous -- flight had begun, 150 million years before any other animal flew.

Diadectes.note: One of the first large plant-eaters on land: a three-metre, barrel-bodied tetrapod with broad cheek teeth, close to the ancestry of reptiles.

Dicranurus.note: A spiny odontopleurid trilobite with two long horns curling back from its head like a ram's.

Dipterus.note: An early lungfish of the Middle Devonian lake of northern Scotland, whose crushing tooth plates are almost those of a living lungfish.

Drepanura.note: A trilobite whose broad, hooked tail shield is the 'swallow stone' of Shandong, collected as a curiosity in China for a thousand years.

Echinosphaerites.note: A cystoid echinoderm, a spiny ball on a short stalk, so abundant in the Middle Ordovician of Baltica that its skeletons form whole beds of limestone.

Elginerpeton.note: One of the earliest tetrapods, known from jaws and limb bones from the Late Devonian of Scotland -- a metre and a half long and still mostly in the water.

Epiphyton.note: A shrub-like calcified microbe that framed reefs with the archaeocyaths in the Cambrian and again in the Late Devonian.

Erbenochile.note: A trilobite with towering eyes crowned by a sunshade -- evidence that it lived in bright, shallow water.

Euproops.note: A small horseshoe crab of the coal-swamp pools, with spined edges to its shield -- a freshwater cousin of the living Limulus.

Falcatus.note: A thirty-centimetre shark of the Bear Gulch lagoon; males carried a spine curving forward over the head like a sickle, used, it seems, in courtship.

Frankea.note: A peri-Gondwanan acritarch with long branching spines, a marker of the cold high-latitude Ordovician seas off North Africa and Iberia.

Fuxianhuia.note: An arthropod of the Chengjiang sea whose brain and nerves were fossilised -- evidence that complex arthropod brains already existed in the Early Cambrian.

Gigantoproductus.note: The largest brachiopod ever: a productid up to thirty centimetres wide, lying in dense shell beds on the Mississippian sea floor.

Gigantoscorpio.note: A Mississippian scorpion some 35 centimetres long from the lake shores of Scotland -- one of the first scorpions certainly built for land.

Gloeocapsomorpha prisca.note: A colonial microbe, probably a cyanobacterium, whose Ordovician blooms made the kukersite oil shale of Estonia -- which still fuels the country's power stations.

Graeophonus.note: A whip spider of the coal forests, with long raptorial forelegs -- the arachnid order has barely changed since.

Greererpeton.note: A long-bodied colosteid with a flat skull and the lateral-line grooves of a fish -- an eel-like hunter that never really left the water.

Harpes.note: A trilobite with a broad, pitted horseshoe brim around its head -- probably a sieve for sifting food from the mud.

Hebertella.note: A ribbed orthid brachiopod, one of the commonest shells of the Late Ordovician seas of Laurentia.

Heliophyllum.note: A large solitary horn coral of the Middle Devonian whose fine growth ridges, counted as days, show about 400 days in a Devonian year.

Hibbertopterus.note: A giant sweep-feeding sea scorpion as long as a person, which raked lake and river beds with its spined limbs; one of its walking trackways runs six metres across a Scottish sandstone.

Holoptychius.note: A porolepiform lobe-finned fish up to two and a half metres long, with big rounded scales and fangs -- one of the commonest large fishes of Late Devonian rivers.

Horneophyton.note: A small plant of the Rhynie hot-spring marsh with a lumpy underground corm and a spore capsule with a central column like a moss's -- from before the vascular plants settled their plan.

Hurdia.note: A radiodont with a long, hood-like carapace over its head -- first described piecemeal as several different animals.

Illaenus.note: A smooth, rounded trilobite that lay half-buried in the sea floor with only its eyes showing -- common on the Ordovician shelves of Baltica.

Isoxys.note: A bivalved Cambrian arthropod with big stalked eyes and spines fore and aft -- a swimming predator found in almost every Cambrian Lagerstätte.

Jaekelopterus.note: The largest arthropod known: a sea scorpion some two and a half metres long, known from a 46-centimetre claw, hunting in Early Devonian estuaries.

Kerygmachela.note: A gilled lobopodian of Sirius Passet with swimming flaps and two long, spined head limbs -- a snapshot of the step from lobopodians to arthropods.

Koninckopora.note: A dasyclad green alga whose calcified branches make up part of many Mississippian limestones.

Kunmingella.note: A millimetre-sized bivalved bradoriid, the most abundant animal of the Chengjiang sea, sometimes preserved with eggs under its shell.

Leanchoilia.note: A megacheiran arthropod with long, whip-tipped 'great appendages' in front, fossilised with its nervous system in the Chengjiang beds.

Lepidophloios.note: A scale tree of the coal swamps whose leaf cushions overlapped like the scales of a cone; it grew as one tall pole, branched once into a crown, shed its spores and died.

Leptophloeum.note: A Late Devonian tree lycopsid with bark patterned in diamonds -- one of the few trees found across Gondwana and the northern continents alike.

Leverhulmia.note: A many-legged myriapod of the Rhynie hot-spring marsh, one of the first animals to walk on land among the first plants.

Lithostrotion.note: A colonial rugose coral whose bundled columns built thickets on the warm Mississippian limestone shelves.

Lycaenops.note: A wolf-sized gorgonopsian with long sabre canines, the kind of predator that hunted dicynodonts across the Late Permian Karoo.

Lyginopteris.note: A scrambling seed fern with glandular hairs on its stems, one of the first plants whose seed-bearing life was worked out from fossils.

Maclurites.note: A big, flat-coiled gastropod with a heavy lid, lying on the Ordovician sea floor like a stone -- its shells stud limestones from Tennessee to Scotland.

Mariopteris.note: A climbing seed fern that hung on tree ferns and scale trees by hooked frond tips -- the lianas of the coal forests.

Mastopora.note: A ball-shaped dasyclad green alga of the Ordovician, like a small calcified sea-grape, common on the carbonate shelves of Laurentia and Baltica.

Materpiscis.note: A 25-centimetre ptyctodont placoderm of the Gogo reef preserved with an embryo and its umbilical cord -- the oldest known live birth.

Mazothairos.note: A palaeodictyopteran with a wingspan of up to half a metre and a sucking beak, from the coal-swamp nodules of Illinois.

Mcnamaraspis.note: A half-metre arthrodire placoderm of the Gogo reef, preserved in three dimensions in limestone nodules -- the state fossil of Western Australia.

Megalograptus.note: One of the largest Ordovician sea scorpions, more than a metre long, with spiny grasping forelimbs.

Meganeuropsis.note: The largest insect known: a griffinfly with wings spanning 71 centimetres, which hunted other insects over the Early Permian coastal plain of Kansas.

Mizzia.note: A green alga built of chains of calcified beads, one of the main sediment-makers of the Permian reef lagoons, from the Capitan reef of Texas to the Tethys.

Nankinolithus.note: A trinucleid trilobite with a broad, pitted fringe around its head -- a sieve for filtering food from the Late Ordovician mud.

Naraoia.note: A soft-shelled, trilobite-like arthropod without eyes or a segmented back -- a naraoiid, common in both the Chengjiang and the Burgess seas.

Neoschwagerina.note: A spindle-shaped fusulinid with a maze of inner walls, the mark of the Middle Permian Tethys -- found in North America only in terranes rafted in from that ocean.

Neuropteris.note: Tongue-shaped leaflets of the medullosan seed ferns, small trees whose fronds reached several metres; they are the commonest plant fossil in the ironstone nodules of the coal measures.

Nuia.note: Tiny calcified rods, probably a green alga, that make up much of the Early Ordovician lime sands of Laurentia and Siberia.

Ogygiocarella.note: A large, flat asaphid trilobite of Avalonia and the Gondwanan margin -- the 'Welsh trilobite', the first trilobite ever figured in print, in 1698.

Ophiacodon.note: A two-to-three-metre synapsid with a long, deep skull -- probably a fish-eater of the Early Permian rivers and swamps.

Orobates.note: A metre-long diadectid known from its skeleton and its own footprints -- enough to rebuild its gait as a robot, which showed it walked more upright than expected.

Pambdelurion.note: A half-metre gilled lobopodian of Sirius Passet, walking and swimming at once, with frontal claws -- a relative of the radiodonts.

Panderichthys.note: A lobe-finned fish of the Middle Devonian lagoons with a flat head, no dorsal fins and the beginnings of fingers in its fin bones.

Parafusulina.note: A large fusulinid: a single cell shaped like a grain of rice, up to a few centimetres long, so common that some Permian limestones are made of little else.

Pareiasaurus.note: A cow-sized, armour-studded plant-eater with leaf-shaped teeth -- one of the pareiasaurs, the largest herbivores of the Late Permian.

Pederpes.note: A metre-long tetrapod from Romer's Gap -- the stretch after the Devonian that had yielded almost no land vertebrates -- with feet that point forward, built for walking.

Pertica.note: A trimerophyte that grew a main stem with side branches in a spiral -- the first hint of the trunk-and-branch plan of trees.

Petrolacosaurus.note: A forty-centimetre, long-limbed reptile of the latest Carboniferous, one of the first diapsids -- the line that later gave lizards, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds.

Phylladoderma.note: A peltasperm seed fern with long, tongue-shaped leaves, typical of the Late Permian floras of the Russian platform and Angara.

Phyllotheca.note: A sphenophyte of the Glossopteris swamps with whorls of long, narrow leaves joined at the base into a collar -- the southern counterpart of Calamites.

Pleurodictyum.note: A small, disc-shaped tabulate coral colony that often grew around a worm living in its base.

Promissum.note: The conodont animal preserved whole: forty centimetres long, eel-like, with big eyes and muscle blocks, from a shale laid down under the end-Ordovician ice.

Proterogyrinus.note: A two-metre anthracosaur of the Mississippian, a long-bodied predator of the swamps from West Virginia to Scotland.

Psilophyton.note: A trimerophyte of the Early Devonian: leafless stems that forked and forked again to a metre tall -- the stock from which ferns, horsetails and seed plants branched.

Pteraspis.note: A jawless fish with a streamlined armoured head shield ending in a long snout, and wing-like spines behind its head that steadied it as it swam.

Renalcis.note: A calcified microbe growing as clusters of tiny chambered lumps -- a builder of reefs beside the archaeocyath sponges in the Cambrian and the stromatoporoids in the Devonian.

Rhacophyton.note: A fern-like plant of the latest Devonian that grew in dense thickets on floodplains -- and burned: charcoal from its wildfires is common in its beds.

Rhinesuchus.note: A two-metre, flat-headed temnospondyl of the Late Permian rivers -- one of the big amphibians that the end-Permian extinction nearly ended.
Rhinesuchus.conf_note: the PBDB's Russian and Indian referrals are doubtful; the genus rests on Karoo material

Rothpletzella.note: Fine calcified filaments that crusted over corals and stromatoporoids on the reefs of the Silurian and Devonian.

Sawdonia.note: A spiny, leafless zosterophyll whose stems uncoiled like fern fiddleheads -- a cousin of the lycopods.

Scutellum.note: A trilobite with a broad, fan-shaped, ribbed tail shield -- a characteristic dweller of Silurian and Devonian reefs.

Scyphocrinites.note: A crinoid that floated from a gas-filled bulb instead of rooting on the sea floor; drifting colonies of it cover whole bedding planes at the Silurian-Devonian boundary.

Sidneyia.note: A thirteen-centimetre Burgess Shale predator whose gut held crushed trilobites and hyoliths.

Sinoceras.note: A long, straight-shelled nautiloid of the Late Ordovician of South China, whose sectioned shells make the 'pagoda stones' of Chinese decorative stone.

Slimonia.note: A metre-long Silurian sea scorpion with a broad body and a spiked tail, from the lagoons of southern Scotland.

Sphenopteridium.note: A Mississippian seed fern with finely divided, wedge-lobed fronds, among the first seed plants to spread across the continents.

Stenodictya.note: A palaeodictyopteran with patterned, net-veined wings and a beak for sucking plant juices, from the coal forests of France.

Stricklandia.note: A large pentamerid brachiopod of the Llandovery whose changing shape through time is used to date Silurian rocks.

Tetradium.note: A colonial coral (or perhaps an alga) of the Ordovician with tubes divided into four, forming mounds in the warm lagoons of Laurentia and Siberia.

Tiktaalik.note: The 'fishapod': a three-metre lobe-finned fish with a neck, a flat head and fins with wrist bones, from Late Devonian river deposits now on Ellesmere Island.

Titanophoneus.note: A carnivorous dinocephalian two and a half metres long, with long canines and a heavy skull -- a top predator of the Middle Permian before the gorgonopsians took over.

Tornoceras.note: A small, smooth goniatite with a zigzag suture, one of the commonest ammonoids of the Middle and Late Devonian seas.

Trimerus.note: A large, smooth homalonotid trilobite with a triangular head, which ploughed through the Silurian and Devonian mud.

Varanops.note: A lightly built, monitor-like synapsid predator a metre and a half long -- one of the last of the early branch of the mammal line.

Vauxia.note: A branching Burgess Shale sponge with a fibrous skeleton -- one of the oldest demosponges.

Ventastega.note: A Late Devonian stem tetrapod from Latvia, between Tiktaalik and Acanthostega -- probably with limbs, still with a fish's tail fin.

Veryhachium.note: A three-to-six-pointed star of an acritarch, the resting cyst of a Palaeozoic plankter, found in marine rocks from the Ordovician to the Permian.

Waagenoceras.note: A goniatite with an intricately frilled suture, from the Middle Permian reef seas of west Texas, Sicily and Timor.

Walliserops.note: A phacopid trilobite with a long three-pronged trident on its head, perhaps used by males in contests.

Waptia.note: A shrimp-like Burgess Shale arthropod that brooded its eggs under its carapace -- the oldest direct evidence of parental care.
Waptia.conf_note: the Chengjiang 'Waptia ovata' is now Chuandianella; Waptia proper is the Burgess Shale species

Westlothiana.note: A slender twenty-centimetre tetrapod from a Mississippian lake shore in Scotland, once hailed as the earliest reptile and now placed just outside the amniotes.

Youngina.note: A small, lizard-shaped diapsid of the latest Permian, close to the common ancestor of lizards and archosaurs; young were found huddled together in a burrow.
